nodes.name: Quantum bit error rate (QBER)
nodes.statement: The crossover probability $q$ of the channel is also known as the QBER.

nodes.name: LDPC code
nodes.statement: One of the ways to perform error correction is to use a LDPC code which is a linear code with a sparse $m\times n$ binary parity-check matrix~\cite{LDPC_orig1,LDPC_orig2}.
differentia: with a sparse $m\times n$ binary parity-check matrix

nodes.name: Syndrome-based LDPC information reconciliation
nodes.statement: Alice multiplies the parity-check matrix by a block of the raw key of length $n$ to obtain a syndrome of length $m$, which is then sent to Bob.~Then, Bob performs a syndrome-decoding operation on his side using his raw key, the same sparse matrix, and an estimated level of QBER, which comes from the preceding procedures.
nodes.statement_short: Alice sends the syndrome of her key block; Bob syndrome-decodes with his raw key and a QBER estimate.
input: a block of the raw key of length $n$
output: the same key as is on Alice's side

nodes.name: Efficiency of a reconciliation protocol
nodes.statement: An important figure of merit for a reconciliation protocol is its efficiency $f$. It is given by the redundancy of disclosed information to the theoretical limit necessary for successful reconciliation~\cite{SlWolf}.

nodes.name: Shannon binary entropy
nodes.statement: For a given BSC it is characterized by the Shannon binary entropy of the QBER~\cite{BinaryEntropy}: \begin{equation} h_\mathrm{b}(q)=-q\log_2q-(1-q)\log_2(1-q). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Efficiency of LDPC reconciliation and code rate
nodes.statement: Thus, the efficiency of the considered information reconciliation with LDPC code can be represented as \begin{equation} f = \frac{m}{nh_\mathrm{b}(q)}=\frac{1-R}{h_\mathrm{b}(q)}, \end{equation} where $R=1-m/n$ is the rate of a given LDPC code.
nodes.statement_short: Efficiency f of fixed-rate LDPC reconciliation equals (1-R)/h_b(q), with code rate R=1-m/n.

nodes.name: Efficiency above unity does not guarantee decoding
nodes.statement: We also note that the efficiency larger than unity does not guarantee successful decoding. In fact, it depends on the specific parity-check matrix, the maximal number of iteration in decoding procedure and other factors.

nodes.name: Extended keys
nodes.statement: The main idea is to perform syndrome coding and decoding with extended keys of length $n$ obtained from the original raw keys of length $n-s-p$ by padding them with $s$ shortened and $p$ punctured bits.
nodes.statement_short: Extended keys of length n are raw keys of length n-s-p padded with s shortened and p punctured bits.

nodes.name: Shortened symbols
nodes.statement: The shortened symbols are the ones which have values exactly known by Alice and Bob, as well as by the adversary.
differentia: which have values exactly known by Alice and Bob, as well as by the adversary

nodes.name: Punctured bits
nodes.statement: The values of punctured bits come from true random number generators (TRNGs), independently of the both sides.

nodes.name: Rate-adaptive LDPC reconciliation (shortening and puncturing)
nodes.statement: After the construction of the extended keys, the parties perform information reconciliation in the same way as discussed above. The difference is that in the case of a successful decoding, Bob excludes shortened and punctured bits from the result of the decoding procedure to obtain a corrected version of his raw key.
nodes.statement_short: Run syndrome reconciliation on the extended keys, then Bob strips shortened and punctured bits from the decoded result.

nodes.name: Efficiency of the rate-adaptive scheme
nodes.statement: The efficiency of the described scheme is defined in the following form: \begin{equation} f = \frac{m-p}{\left[n-p-s\right]h_\mathrm{b}(q)}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Shortening and puncturing tune efficiency
nodes.statement: Thus, the artificial reduction (increase) of discrepancies between extended keys by shortened (punctured) bits allows one to implement fine-tuning of efficiency in order to keep a trade-off between a probability of failure for belief-propagation decoding and information leakage.

nodes.name: Blind reconciliation
nodes.statement: Blind reconciliation is based on the hybrid automatic repeat request technique~\cite{HARQ} with the LDPC codes with an essential presence of punctured symbols. The crucial difference is that, in the case of a decoding failure, parties try to implement the decoding procedure again by turning a number of punctured symbols into shortened ones instead of discarding their blocks.~The values of these bits are transferred via the classical channel after a corresponding request of Bob.~Once the punctured bits are exhausted it is possible to continue revealing additional information with sifted key bits.
nodes.statement_short: HARQ-style LDPC reconciliation: on decoding failure, punctured symbols are turned into shortened ones by revealing their values, then sifted key bits.

nodes.name: Efficiency of blind reconciliation
nodes.statement: The efficiency of the procedure after $n_\mathrm{add}$ number of additional communication rounds is given by~\cite{LDPC5_blind} \begin{equation} f = \frac{m-p_0+n_\mathrm{add}d}{\left[n-p_0-s_0\right]h_\mathrm{b}(q)}, \end{equation} where $s_0$ and $p_0$ are the initial numbers of punctured and shortened bits, and $d$ is the number of disclosed bits in each additional round of blind reconciliation.
nodes.statement_short: Efficiency after n_add extra rounds, each disclosing d bits, starting from s0 shortened and p0 punctured bits.

nodes.name: Meaning of the blind-reconciliation efficiency
nodes.statement: The meaning of expression~\eqref{eq:fadapt} relative to with expression~\eqref{eq:fad} is as follows: if the decoding procedure according to the rate-adaptive scheme with efficiency~\eqref{eq:fad} does not converge, then the parties increase $f$ in each additional communication round of the blind reconciliation to increase the probability of convergence.

nodes.name: Symmetric blind information reconciliation
nodes.statement: First, in analogy to the rate-adaptive scheme, the parties choose the numbers and positions of the shortened and punctured bits and extend their blocks of raw keys. Second, both Alice and Bob compute the syndrome of their extended raw keys and share them with each other. Then they perform belief-propagation decoding. In a successful case, one party --- say Bob --- corrects the errors, and the procedure proceeds to the verification stage. In failed case, the parties exchange the values of a fixed number of bits having maximal uncertainty according to the log-likelihood ratio (LLR). After that, Alice and Bob repeat the belief-propagation decoding procedure with the updated list of shortened and punctured positions.
nodes.statement_short: Both parties exchange syndromes of extended keys and run BP decoding; on failure they reveal the bits with lowest |LLR| and retry.

nodes.name: Disclosed positions chosen by failed decoding
nodes.statement: The alternative ingredient is that the positions of additionally disclosed bits come not from the punctured positions but are decidedly indicated by an unsuccessful belief-propagation decoding algorithm.~This removes the restrictions on a number of additionally disclosed bits and also makes it possible to perform interactive LDPC code-based reconciliation even in the absence of punctured bits. The latter scenario allows the adjustment of current sets of LDPC codes to a broad range of QBER values (see Appendix A).
nodes.statement_short: Unlike blind reconciliation, revealed positions come from the failed decoding, removing the limit on disclosed bits and the need for punctured bits.

nodes.name: Simultaneous messages
nodes.statement: We also note that, in contrast to the standard blind reconciliation protocol, where the parties use two consecutive messages in each of the communication rounds (the request and the corresponding answer), in the symmetric blind reconciliation the messages between parties are transferred simultaneously.

nodes.name: Guaranteed convergence of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement: The convergence of the proposed method is formally guaranteed by the fact that, in the worst-case scenario, the parties reveal the entire extended key.
conclusions: The convergence of the proposed method is formally guaranteed

nodes.name: Efficiency of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement: The efficiency of the suggested method as of blind reconciliation is given by Eq. \eqref{eq:fadapt}.
conclusions: The efficiency of the suggested method as of blind reconciliation is given by Eq. \eqref{eq:fadapt}.

nodes.name: Lo's security analysis applies to symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement: It turns out that the symmetric blind reconciliation due to its inherent symmetry has a lot in common with the Cascade method, and the security analysis, developed for a class of adaptive symmetric error-correction methods (including the Cascade method) given in Ref.~\cite{LO_decoupling}, is applicable to our proposed scheme as well.
conclusions: the security analysis, developed for a class of adaptive symmetric error-correction methods (including the Cascade method) given in Ref.~\cite{LO_decoupling}, is applicable to our proposed scheme as well.

nodes.name: Standard LDPC code set
nodes.statement: We use a set of four standard LDPC codes~\cite{Standard} with the rates \begin{equation} \mathcal{R} = \{5/6, 3/4, 2/3, 1/2\}, \end{equation} with the block length fixed to $n=1944$.

nodes.name: Untainted-puncturing position lists
nodes.statement: For each of these codes, we obtain a list of bit positions according to the untainted-puncturing technique~\cite{UntP} containing $p_{\max}=$ 154, 221, 295 and 433 symbols, respectively.

nodes.name: Number of disclosed bits per round
nodes.statement: The number of bits to be disclosed in each additional round of the procedure is chosen according to a particular code rate $R$ and the heuristic expression \begin{equation} d(R) = \lceil n\cdot(0.0280-0.02R) \cdot \alpha \rceil , \end{equation} where $n$ is the block length, $\alpha$ is the auxiliary parameter, and $\lceil\dots\rceil$ is the standard ceiling operation.
nodes.statement_short: Heuristic number d(R) of bits disclosed per extra round, scaled by an auxiliary parameter alpha.

nodes.name: Symmetric scheme improves efficiency and rounds (simulation)
nodes.statement: First, one can see that symmetric reconciliation improves both efficiencies $f$.~This comes from the fact that the decoding procedure in the symmetric scheme has a faster convergence rate.~Moreover, it requires a smaller number of additional communication rounds.
conclusions: it requires a smaller number of additional communication rounds

nodes.name: Average 10% efficiency and 30% request improvement
nodes.statement: From these data, we identify an average of ${10}\%$ improvement in the efficiency ($10.4\%$ for $\alpha = 1$, and $11.4\%$ for $\alpha=0.5$) and an average of ${30}\%$ improvement in the number of information requests ($28\%$ for $\alpha=1$, and $33\%$ for $\alpha=0.5$).
conclusions: an average of ${10}\%$ improvement in the efficiency
an average of ${30}\%$ improvement in the number of information requests

nodes.name: No frame errors from failed decodings
nodes.statement: Moreover, the scheme does not suffer from the frame errors coming from unsuccessful belief-propagation decodings.
conclusions: the scheme does not suffer from the frame errors coming from unsuccessful belief-propagation decodings

nodes.name: Extended LDPC code-rate set
nodes.statement: The second set of codes has rates in the range \begin{equation} \mathcal{R}'=\{0.5,0.55,\ldots,0.9\} \end{equation} with the block length fixed to $n{=}4000$.

nodes.name: Short codes with small alpha match long codes
nodes.statement: It is clearly seen that the use of codes with block length $n=1944$ and $\alpha=0.5$ gives roughly the same efficiency as the codes with the block length $n=4000$ and $\alpha=1$.
conclusions: gives roughly the same efficiency as the codes with the block length $n=4000$ and $\alpha=1$

nodes.name: Illustrative industrial QKD example
nodes.statement: In order to evaluate the performance of our proposed scheme in the context of industrial QKD systems, we consider an illustrative example based on the results of Ref.~\cite{Gisin2}. In this particular setup, the information reconciliation was performed with a straightforward implementation of the standard $n=1944$ LDPC code~\cite{Standard} with $R=3/4$ using QBER $q\approx 1.9\%$. According to the results presented in Fig.~\ref{fig:full_qber}, an implementation of symmetric blind reconciliation may lead to a decrease of efficiency down to $f\approx 1.3$ with approximately six additional communication rounds. It provides a $10\%$ increase in the secure key rate (we note that Cascade implementation of the information reconciliation procedure in the same conditions requires about $50$ communication rounds~\cite{Cascade2_rev}).
nodes.statement_short: For the n=1944, R=3/4 setup at q~1.9%, symmetric blind reconciliation reaches f~1.3 in ~6 rounds, a 10% key-rate gain.

nodes.name: Workflow of the symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement: First, we assume that Alice and Bob have an estimated value of QBER $q_\mathrm{est}$, which comes from the preceding error estimation step or previous rounds of post-processing procedure. Parties start with choosing the optimal code from a set (pool) of available LDPC codes according to $q_\mathrm{est}$ and desired starting efficiency $f_{\mathrm{start}}$ (in all of our discussions, it is set to unity). For each code, specified by its $m\times n$ parity matrix $\mathbf{H}$ (with $m<n$), parties calculate the number of shortened ($s$) or punctured $(p)$ symbols that is required to obtain desired efficiency $f_{\mathrm{start}}$ from the nonadaptable efficiency $f_0=m/\left[n\;h_\mathrm{b}(q_\mathrm{est})\right]$ as follows: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & p=\lfloor {(m- nh_\mathrm{b}(q_\mathrm{est})f_{\mathrm{start}})}/{(1-h_\mathrm{b}(q_\mathrm{est})f_{\mathrm{start}})} \rfloor, \\ & s=0 \end{aligned} \end{equation} for $f_0>f_{\mathrm{start}}$, and \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & s= \lceil n - m/h_\mathrm{b}(q_\mathrm{est})f_{\mathrm{start}}\rceil, \\ & p=0 \end{aligned} \end{equation} for $f_0<f_{\mathrm{start}}$. The particular code among the set is then chosen in such a way that it has the maximal number of raw key bits in the extended key. We note that, in our approach, we use only shortened {\it or} punctured bits to obtain the desired efficiency $f_{\mathrm{start}}$ [see also Fig.~\ref{fig:methods}(b)]. This method is quite different from the commonly used approach~\cite{LDPC4_adapt1,LDPC4_adapt2}, where the sum of the numbers of shortened and punctured bits remains constant. Then the parties take blocks of their raw keys $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ of length $n-p-s$ and pad them with shortened and punctured symbols obtaining extended keys $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $\mathbf{y}_{\mathrm{ext}}$ of code block length $n$. In Fig.~\ref{fig:methods}(a) we denote this operation as $E(\cdot, S, P)$, where $S$ and $P$ are lists of positions for shortened and punctured symbols of length $s$ and $p$, respectively. If it is possible, parties choose $P$ using position from special list, generated in advance with untainted puncturing technique~\cite{UntP}. Otherwise, the parties choose $P$ as well as $S$ with a synchronized PRNG. All shortened symbols obtains zero values, while the values of the punctured bits come from the TRNG (independently on each side). The party that modifies its raw key (in our case it is Bob) also keeps original positions of shortened and punctured symbols as $S_0$ and $P_0$. These position are used in the final stage of the procedure. The subsequent part of the procedure aims at reconstruction of a vector $\mathbf{e}_\mathrm{dec}$, which we call an error pattern, such that \begin{equation} \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbf{y}_{\mathrm{ext}}+\mathbf{e}_\mathrm{dec} ~ (\mathrm{mod}~2). \end{equation} In order to cope with this task, both Alice and Bob initialize the supposed error pattern $\mathbf{e}$ as the zero vector, calculate the syndromes $\mathbf{s_x}$ and $\mathbf{s_y}$ of their extended keys $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $\mathbf{y}_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and share the obtained syndromes with each other. Then each party performs belief-propagation decoding with the relative syndrome \begin{equation} \mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s_x}+\mathbf{s_y}~(\mathrm{mod}~2). \end{equation} We use an updated belief-propagation decoding algorithm (see below), which returns not only a resulting decoded vector $\mathbf{e}_\mathrm{dec}$ (that is ``none'' in the failure case), but also a set of bit positions $D$ of a fixed length $d$ which have the lowest LLR upon completion of the decoding. In other words, the updated decoding procedure returns $d$ positions of symbols with the most uncertainty in their values. Owing to the fact that both parties perform the same operation, they obtain the same output $\mathbf{e}_\mathrm{dec}$ and $D$. In the case of a failure ($\mathbf{e}_\mathrm{dec}=\mathrm{none}$), the parties share the values of bits in the positions of $D$, update their supposed error pattern $\mathbf{e}$ in the positions from $D$ according to received values, \begin{equation} \mathbf{e}[D] = \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}}[D]+\mathbf{y}_{\mathrm{ext}}[D]~(\mathrm{mod}~2), \end{equation} and try to perform the decoding process again by marking positions in $D$ as shortened, which is crucial for the subsequent decoding procedure. This sequence of operations is repeated until a convergence of belief-propagation decoding. Then Bob applies error correction according to the obtained error pattern $\mathbf{e}_\mathrm{dec}$ by modulo 2 summation with his extended key $\mathbf{y}$. Finally, Bob excludes the symbols with initially shortened $S_0$ and punctured $P_0$ positions to obtain the corrected key $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{dec}}$ [we denote this operation $E^{-1}$ in Fig.~\ref{fig:methods}(a)], and parties move to the verification step with the original raw key $\mathbf{x}$ on Alice's side and its corrected version $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{dec}}$ on Bob's one.

input: blocks of their raw keys $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$
output: the original raw key $\mathbf{x}$ on Alice's side and its corrected version $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{dec}}$ on Bob's one
nodes.statement_short: Detailed protocol: pick code and shortened/punctured counts for f_start, exchange syndromes, BP-decode the relative syndrome, reveal lowest-LLR bits until convergence. Key step: disclosed positions D come from the failed decoding.

nodes.name: Log-likelihood ratio (LLR)
nodes.statement: For a given random bit variable $X$, its LLR is defined as \begin{equation} \mathrm{LLR}(X) \equiv \log\frac{\mathrm{Prob}(X=0)}{\mathrm{Prob}(X=1)}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Symbol nodes and check nodes
nodes.statement: It consists of $n$ \emph{symbol nodes} and $m$ \emph{check nodes} that corresponds to rows and columns of parity-check matrix $\mathbf{H}$.

nodes.name: Tanner graph adjacency
nodes.statement: The $i$-th symbol node is connected by edge with the $j$-th check node if and only if the corresponding element of parity-check matrix is nonzero: $\mathbf{H}[i,j]=1$.

nodes.name: Decoding procedure decode
nodes.statement: We consider the decoding procedure as follows: \begin{equation} \mathbf{e}_\mathrm{dec}, D:=\mathrm{decode}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{e}, \mathbf{H},q_\mathrm{est}, S, P), \end{equation} where $\mathbf{s}$ is the syndrome, $\mathbf{e}$ is the vector of length $n$ that has to be corrected, $\mathbf{H}$ is the $m\times n$ parity-check matrix, $q_\mathrm{est}$ is the estimated level of crossover probability (QBER), $S$ and $P$ are positions of shortened and punctured bits, $\mathbf{e}_\mathrm{dec}$ is the corrected version of $\mathbf{e}$, and $D$ is the list of positions for $d$ symbols with the lowest LLR values, where $d$ is considered as an external constant.
nodes.statement_short: decode(s,e,H,q_est,S,P) returns the corrected vector e_dec and the d positions D with lowest LLR.

nodes.name: Updated belief-propagation sum-product decoding
nodes.statement: The workflow of the procedure is as follows. We with a calculation of the initial LLRs for all symbol nodes. The corresponding vector is denoted as $\mathbf{r}^{(0)}$ and its elements are given by \begin{equation} \mathbf{r}^{(0)}[i] := \begin{cases} (-1)^{\mathbf{e}[i]} r_\mathrm{k}, &i\in K \\ (-1)^{\mathbf{e}[i]} r_\mathrm{s}, &i\in S \\ 0, &i\in P \end{cases}, \end{equation} where $K$ consists of raw key positions, such that \begin{equation} K\cup S\cup P=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}. \end{equation} Here, $r_\mathrm{k}$ is calculated using an estimated value of QBER, $\epsilon_\mathrm{est}$: \begin{equation} r_\mathrm{k} = \log\frac{1-q_\mathrm{est}}{q_\mathrm{est}}. \end{equation} The LLR value for shortened symbols $r_\mathrm{s}\gg 1$ and, in our implementation, we use $r_\mathrm{s}:=100$. The LLR for punctured symbols is zero, as there is no information about their values since they come from an independent true RNG The initial messages from check nodes to symbol nodes are given by the initial values of corresponding LLRs as follows: \begin{equation} \mathbf{M}_{i\rightarrow j}^{(1)} := \mathbf{r}^{(0)}[i]. \end{equation} Here $i\in \mathcal{N}$ and $j\in A_i$, where $A_i$ is a set of symbol nodes connected to the $i$-th symbol node. Check nodes from messages back to the symbol node are realized in the following way: \begin{equation} \mathbf{M}_{i\leftarrow j}^{(k)} := 2\tanh^{-1}\left[\prod_{i'\in B_j/i}\frac{\mathbf{M}_{i'\rightarrow j}^{(k)}}{2}\right](-1)^{\mathbf{s}[j]}, \end{equation} where $j\in\mathcal{M}\equiv\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and $i\in B_j$, with $B_j$ being a set of symbol nodes connected to the $j$-th check node. We note that $\mathbf{M}_{i\leftarrow j}$ does not take into account $\mathbf{M}_{i\rightarrow j}$. Actually $\mathbf{M}_{i\leftarrow j}$ is the LLR of the $i$-th bit value based on satisfying the parity equation of the $j$-th row of the parity-check matrix $\mathbf{H}$, and the LLRs of all other symbol nodes taking part in this equation [see Fig.~\ref{fig:methods}(d)]. The symbol node updates its LLR using all of the messages coming from its check nodes: \begin{equation} \mathbf{r}^{(k)}[i] := \mathbf{r}^{(0)}[i]+\sum_{j\in A_i} \mathbf{M}_{i\leftarrow j}^{(k)} \end{equation} and it calculates current estimates for the bit values, \begin{equation} \mathbf{z}^{(k)}[i] := \begin{cases} 0, &\mathbf{r}^{(k)}[i]\geq0 \\ 1, &\mathbf{r}^{(k)}[i]<0 \end{cases}. \end{equation} If this estimate satisfies all parity equations, \begin{equation} \mathbf{H}\mathbf{z}^{(k)}=\mathbf{s}~(\mathrm{mod}~2), \end{equation} then the algorithm stops and returns the decoded vector $\mathbf{z}$ As a stopping criterion, we consider behavior of averaged magnitude LLRs for symbols in nonshortened positions: \begin{equation} \hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(k)}:=\frac{1}{n-s}\sum_{i\in K\cup P}|\mathbf{r}^{(k)}[i]|. \end{equation} We stop the decoding and return ``none'' as the decoded vector if, for the current step $k$, the following inequality holds: \begin{equation} \hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(k)}\leq\frac{1}{\mathcal{N}}\sum_{j=k-\mathcal{N}}^{k-1}\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(j)}, \end{equation} where we use $\mathcal{N}:=5$. It can be interpreted as the end of a growth trend as far as our confidence in bit values. The algorithm also returns a $D$ that is a list of $d$ positions of symbols which has minimal values of LLR magnitude \begin{equation} D = \{i\;|\;|\mathbf{r}^{(k)}[i]|\leq |\mathbf{r}^{(k)}[j]| ~\forall j\notin D \}, \quad |D| = d. \end{equation} Otherwise, the algorithm goes to the next step. According to the new LLRs, we update the messages from the symbol nodes to the check nodes: \begin{equation} \begin{split} \mathbf{M}_{i\rightarrow j}^{(k+1)} &:= \mathbf{r}^{(0)}[i]+\sum_{j'\in A_i/j} \mathbf{M}_{i\leftarrow j'}^{(k)} \\ &= \mathbf{r}^{(k)}[i]-\mathbf{M}_{i\leftarrow j}^{(k)} \end{split} \end{equation} where the counter of iterations is incremented, $k:=k+1$ [see Fig.~\ref{fig:methods}(e)], and the algorithm goes to the step with check nodes from messages back to symbol node [see Eq. (\ref{eq:step3})].
output: a $D$ that is a list of $d$ positions of symbols which has minimal values of LLR magnitude
nodes.statement_short: LLR sum-product BP decoding with a stopping rule on averaged |LLR| growth, returning also the d least reliable positions.

nodes.name: Optimizing check-node computation
nodes.statement: It is important to note that the most computationally expensive calculation~(\ref{eq:Mes}) can be optimized by using a technique suggested in Ref.~\cite{Decodoptim}.

nodes.name: Punctured symbols deactivate check nodes
nodes.statement: We also point out that Eq.~(\ref{eq:Mes}) reveals some peculiarity regarding punctured symbols. A zero LLR of the punctured symbol $i\in B_j$ on the first step ``deactivates'' the $j$th check node making all messages $\mathbf{M}_{i'\leftarrow j}$ ($i'\in B_j$, $i'\neq i$) to other symbol nodes to be zero. If there are no punctured bits in $B_j/i$, then $|\mathbf{M}_{i\leftarrow j}|>0$, and the $i$th node is ``rescued'' after the first iteration and then participates in the decoding procedure. However, if there are at least two punctured nodes connected to a given $j$th check node, then all messages $\mathbf{M}_{i\leftarrow j}, i\in B_j$ are zero. There still a possibility that the punctures symbols will be 'rescued' via another check nodes, but such behavior nonetheless indicates the importance of choosing a set of punctured symbols. To avoid this situation the special technique of untainted puncturing is used~\cite{UntP}.
nodes.statement_short: A zero-LLR punctured symbol zeroes a check node's outgoing messages; two punctured symbols on one check node block it, motivating untainted puncturing.

nodes.name: Information leakage of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement: Specifically, we show that the amount of information leakage have to be taken into account in the privacy amplification step in accordance with Eq.\eqref{eq:fadapt} is given by \begin{equation} {\rm leak}_{\rm ec}=m-p_0+n_\mathrm{add}\;d, \end{equation} where recall $m$ is the syndrome length, $p_0$ is the initial number of punctured symbols, $n_\mathrm{add}$ is the number of additional communication rounds, and $d$ is the number of bits disclosed in each of these rounds.
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
conclusions: the amount of information leakage have to be taken into account in the privacy amplification step in accordance with Eq.\eqref{eq:fadapt} is given by
nodes.statement_short: The leakage to account for in privacy amplification is m - p0 + n_add d.

nodes.name: Proof of the leakage formula
nodes.statement: During the symmetric blind reconciliation Alice and Bob exchange \begin{equation} \mathcal{L} = 2(m+n_\mathrm{add}\;d) \end{equation} bits of information: each party transfers an $m$-bit syndrome and $n_\mathrm{add}\;d$ bits in additional communication rounds. Obviously, the information leakage could not be larger than $\mathcal{L}$. Nevertheless, the actual leakage turns out to be lower (and given by Eq.\eqref{eq:leak}) for two reasons. First is that the $p_0$ punctured symbols due to their inherent uncertainty decrease the leakage from each of the syndromes from $m$ to $m-p_0$; and second is that the factor 2 in~\eqref{eq:len} could be omitted due to the fact that each pair of parity bits (one transferring from Alice to Bob, and the other -- in the opposite direction) can bring only one bit of valuable information to the eavesdropper. Next, we would like to focus on these two points. Let us consider a symmetric blind reconciliation protocol for ${m}\times{n}$ parity-check matrix, $(n-s_0-p_0)$-bit sifted keys, $s_0$ shortened, and $p_0$ punctured bits. Recall that the punctured symbols are the bits with values coming from independent TRNGs on both sides. The consideration of the puncturing technique is greatly simplified in untainted puncturing ~\cite{UntP}, which is employed in our scheme. In the untainted puncturing, each of the check nodes of the Tanner graph (corresponding the employed parity-check matrix) is connected with, at most, one punctured symbol. This implies that it is possible to split al ofl the syndrome bits' positions $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ into the subsets $F$ and $\overline{F}$ where $F$ contains $p_0$ check nodes indices of those which are connected with the punctured bits, and the subset $\overline{F}\equiv \{1,2,\ldots,m\}/F$ contains all of the remaining syndrome-bit positions. Since each of the syndrome-bit values $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{x}}[F]$ and $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{y}}[F]$ is obtained as the result of a modulo-2 summation of nonpunctured symbols and a single punctured bit (which is completely random at each side), the disclosure of $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{x}}[F]$ and $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{y}}[F]$ in the public channel does not bring any valuable information to the eavesdropper. One can imagine that bits of $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{x}}[F]$ and $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{y}}[F]$ are transferred separately from all other public communications that is considered further. Thus, the information leakage does not exceed $2(m-p_0+n_\mathrm{add}\;d)$ bits. We wish to remark that the case of random puncturing, where the \emph{positions} for punctured symbols are chosen with synchronised PRNGs, could be treated in a similar way, but in this case an additional information about the Tanner graph construction method has to be taken into account. One has to show that it is always possible to choose $p_0$ syndrome bits whose values are statistically independent from the $n-p_0$ values of symbols that are not punctured. The second statement about the factor 2 in Eq.~\eqref{eq:len} is closely related to a similar question regarding to the one of the first information reconciliation protocols -- Cascade~\cite{Cascade1_orig}, where Alice and Bob also exchange with parity bits of some blocks of their keys in a symmetrical way. A rigorous examination of this question related to the BB84 protocol is considered by H.-K. Lo in Ref.~\cite{LO_decoupling}. In his work Lo considers the \emph{adaptive symmetric method for error correction} (which we will refer to simply as \emph{adaptive symmetric error correction}) --- the generalized information reconciliation protocol which includes Cascade and the symmetric blind reconciliation. Next, we provide its definition. \emph{Definition}~(adapted from Ref.~\cite{LO_decoupling}). Adaptive symmetric error correction is an iterative procedure applied to Alice's $n$-bit string $\mathbf{x}$ and Bob's $n$-bit string $\mathbf{y}$ (which is a corrupted version of $\mathbf{x}$). where the rounds of operations given below are performed. \begin{itemize} \item Round 1. Alice picks an $n$-bit string ${\bf a}_1$, and broadcasts ${\bf a}_1$ and the parity $p_{\mathbf{x},1} = {\bf a}_1 \cdot \mathbf{x}~({\rm mod}~2)$. Bob broadcasts the parity $p_{\mathbf{y},1} = {\bf a}_1 \cdot \mathbf{y}~({\rm mod}~2)$. Alice and Bob compute the relative parity $r_1=p_{\mathbf{y},1}-p_{\mathbf{x},1}~({\rm mod}~2)$. \item Round $i$ ($i>1$). Alice picks an $i$-bit string ${\bf a}_i$, where the choice of ${\bf a}_i$ may depend on the strings $\{{\bf a}_j|j<i\}$ and the relative parities $\{r_j|j<i\}$ (but not on the individual parities, $\{p_{\mathbf{x},j}|j<i\}$ and $\{p_{\mathbf{y},j}|j<i\}$). Then Alice broadcasts ${\bf a}_i$ and the parity $p_{\mathbf{x},i} = {\bf a}_i \cdot \mathbf{x}~({\rm mod}~2)$. Bob broadcasts the parity $p_{y,i} = {\bf a}_i \cdot \mathbf{y}~({\rm mod}~2)$. Alice and Bob compute the relative parity $r_i=p_{\mathbf{y},1}-p_{\mathbf{x},1}~({\rm mod}~2)$. \end{itemize} After some number $N$ of necessary rounds, Bob corrects the errors in his string $\mathbf{y}$ by applying a recovery operator \begin{equation} \mathbf{z}:=\mathrm{Recover}(\mathbf{y}, \{r_i\}_{i=1}^N). \end{equation} Ideally, $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{x}$ and Alice and Bob will now share the same string $\mathbf{x}$. One can see that, in the described protocol, Alice and Bob exchange with $2N$ bits of information: $N$ bits goes from Alice to Bob, and $N$ bits -- in the opposite direction. In Ref.~\cite{LO_decoupling} it was proven that the procedure of adaptive symmetric error correction is secure for purposes of the BB84 QKD protocol in the case where both parity bits $p_{\mathbf{x},i}$ and $p_{\mathbf{y},i}$ are both one-time pad encrypted with the \emph{same} secret bit. That is, Alice and Bob exchange with the messages $p_{\mathbf{x},i}+\mathbf{w}[i]~({\rm mod}~2)$ and $p_{\mathbf{y},i}+\mathbf{w}[i]~({\rm mod}~2)$, where $\mathbf{w}$ is an $n$-bit string of the secret key possessed by Alice and Bob. From an overall key generation balance point of view, this scenario is equivalent to the situation, where the information leakage in the adaptive symmetric error correction is equal to $N$. Now we return to the symmetric blind reconciliation. As it was shown, the communication of $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{x}}[F]$ and $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{y}}[F]$ can be considered separately since none of these bits bring any valuable information to the eavesdropper. The exchange of the remaining syndrome bits $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{x}}[\overline{F}]$ and $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{y}}[\overline{F}]$, can be regarded as the first $m-p_0$ rounds of the adaptive symmetric error correction: for each syndrome bit, the string ${\bf a}_i$ from the definition is the corresponding row of the employed parity-check matrix. The syndrome decoding algorithm~\eqref{eq:synddec} either converges and allows Bob to perform a recovery of $\mathbf{x}$ or returns a set of positions $D$ for the new communication round. Note that the set $D$ is obtained as a result of the syndrome decoding executed for the relative syndrome $\mathbf{s}$. By its definition [see Eq.~\eqref{eq:relsyndr}], the relative syndrome consists of relative parities; therefore the choice of positions for the set $D$ is in agreement with the definition of adaptive symmetric error correction. Each of the additional communication rounds of the symmetric blind reconciliation with respect to the set $D$, can be regarded as $|D|=d$ of communication rounds in the definition of the adaptive symmetric error correction. Namely, the string ${\bf a}_i$ has all zeros except for a single one at the position $D_j$ (here, $i$ is the number of the round in the general sequence, and $j$ is the index of the element inside the set $D$ of length $d$). Thus, the completion of the symmetric blind reconciliation with $n_{\rm add}$ additional rounds corresponds to the adaptive symmetric error correction with $N=m-p_0+n_{\rm add}d$ rounds, and the information leakage given by expression~\eqref{eq:leak}.
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Untainted-punctured syndrome bits leak nothing, and the protocol is an instance of Lo's adaptive symmetric error correction, whose leakage equals the number of rounds N=m-p0+n_add d.

Alice picks an $n$-bit string ${\bf a}_1$, and broadcasts ${\bf a}_1$ and the parity $p_{\mathbf{x},1} = {\bf a}_1 \cdot \mathbf{x}~({\rm mod}~2)$. Alice and Bob compute the relative parity $r_1=p_{\mathbf{y},1}-p_{\mathbf{x},1}~({\rm mod}~2)$. \item Round $i$ ($i>1$). Alice picks an $i$-bit string ${\bf a}_i$, where the choice of ${\bf a}_i$ may depend on the strings $\{{\bf a}_j|j<i\}$ and the relative parities $\{r_j|j<i\}$ (but not on the individual parities, $\{p_{\mathbf{x},j}|j<i\}$ and $\{p_{\mathbf{y},j}|j<i\}$). Then Alice broadcasts ${\bf a}_i$ and the parity $p_{\mathbf{x},i} = {\bf a}_i \cdot \mathbf{x}~({\rm mod}~2)$. Bob broadcasts the parity $p_{y,i} = {\bf a}_i \cdot \mathbf{y}~({\rm mod}~2)$. nodes.statement_short: Rounds where Alice broadcasts a string a_i (chosen from past relative parities) and both broadcast parities a_i.x, a_i.y; Bob then recovers x.

nodes.name: Security of adaptive symmetric error correction (Lo)
nodes.statement: In Ref.~\cite{LO_decoupling} it was proven that the procedure of adaptive symmetric error correction is secure for purposes of the BB84 QKD protocol in the case where both parity bits $p_{\mathbf{x},i}$ and $p_{\mathbf{y},i}$ are both one-time pad encrypted with the \emph{same} secret bit. That is, Alice and Bob exchange with the messages $p_{\mathbf{x},i}+\mathbf{w}[i]~({\rm mod}~2)$ and $p_{\mathbf{y},i}+\mathbf{w}[i]~({\rm mod}~2)$, where $\mathbf{w}$ is an $n$-bit string of the secret key possessed by Alice and Bob.
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
assumptions: both parity bits $p_{\mathbf{x},i}$ and $p_{\mathbf{y},i}$ are both one-time pad encrypted with the \emph{same} secret bit
conclusions: the procedure of adaptive symmetric error correction is secure for purposes of the BB84 QKD protocol

nodes.name: Alice computes and sends syndrome
nodes.statement: Alice multiplies the parity-check matrix by a block of the raw key of length $n$ to obtain a syndrome of length $m$, which is then sent to Bob.
nodes.statement_short: Alice computes the syndrome of her key block and sends it.

nodes.name: Bob syndrome-decodes
nodes.statement: Then, Bob performs a syndrome-decoding operation on his side using his raw key, the same sparse matrix, and an estimated level of QBER, which comes from the preceding procedures.
nodes.statement_short: Bob decodes using his raw key, the matrix and the QBER estimate.

nodes.name: Reconcile extended keys
nodes.statement: After the construction of the extended keys, the parties perform information reconciliation in the same way as discussed above.
nodes.statement_short: Run standard syndrome reconciliation on extended keys.

nodes.name: Strip shortened and punctured bits
nodes.statement: The difference is that in the case of a successful decoding, Bob excludes shortened and punctured bits from the result of the decoding procedure to obtain a corrected version of his raw key.
nodes.statement_short: Bob removes shortened and punctured bits from the decoded key.

nodes.name: Turn punctured into shortened
nodes.statement: The crucial difference is that, in the case of a decoding failure, parties try to implement the decoding procedure again by turning a number of punctured symbols into shortened ones instead of discarding their blocks.
nodes.statement_short: On failure, convert some punctured symbols into shortened ones and retry decoding.

nodes.name: Transfer values on request
nodes.statement: The values of these bits are transferred via the classical channel after a corresponding request of Bob.
nodes.statement_short: Alice sends the converted bits' values on Bob's request.

nodes.name: Reveal sifted key bits
nodes.statement: Once the punctured bits are exhausted it is possible to continue revealing additional information with sifted key bits.
nodes.statement_short: After punctured bits run out, reveal sifted key bits.

nodes.name: Extend raw keys
nodes.statement: First, in analogy to the rate-adaptive scheme, the parties choose the numbers and positions of the shortened and punctured bits and extend their blocks of raw keys.
nodes.statement_short: Choose shortened/punctured positions and extend the raw-key blocks.

nodes.name: Exchange syndromes
nodes.statement: Second, both Alice and Bob compute the syndrome of their extended raw keys and share them with each other.
nodes.statement_short: Both parties compute and exchange syndromes.

nodes.name: BP decoding
nodes.statement: Then they perform belief-propagation decoding.
nodes.statement_short: Run belief-propagation decoding.

nodes.name: Success branch
nodes.statement: In a successful case, one party --- say Bob --- corrects the errors, and the procedure proceeds to the verification stage.
nodes.statement_short: On success Bob corrects errors and goes to verification.

nodes.name: Failure branch
nodes.statement: In failed case, the parties exchange the values of a fixed number of bits having maximal uncertainty according to the log-likelihood ratio (LLR).
nodes.statement_short: On failure exchange values of the bits with maximal LLR uncertainty.

nodes.name: Repeat decoding
nodes.statement: After that, Alice and Bob repeat the belief-propagation decoding procedure with the updated list of shortened and punctured positions.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat decoding with updated shortened/punctured lists.

nodes.name: QBER estimate
nodes.statement: First, we assume that Alice and Bob have an estimated value of QBER $q_\mathrm{est}$, which comes from the preceding error estimation step or previous rounds of post-processing procedure.
nodes.section: Appendix A: Workflow of the symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Start from an estimated QBER.

nodes.name: Choose code
nodes.statement: Parties start with choosing the optimal code from a set (pool) of available LDPC codes according to $q_\mathrm{est}$ and desired starting efficiency $f_{\mathrm{start}}$ (in all of our discussions, it is set to unity).
nodes.section: Appendix A: Workflow of the symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Choose a code from the pool for q_est and f_start.

nodes.name: Compute shortened/punctured counts
nodes.statement: For each code, specified by its $m\times n$ parity matrix $\mathbf{H}$ (with $m<n$), parties calculate the number of shortened ($s$) or punctured $(p)$ symbols that is required to obtain desired efficiency $f_{\mathrm{start}}$ from the nonadaptable efficiency $f_0=m/\left[n\;h_\mathrm{b}(q_\mathrm{est})\right]$ as follows: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & p=\lfloor {(m- nh_\mathrm{b}(q_\mathrm{est})f_{\mathrm{start}})}/{(1-h_\mathrm{b}(q_\mathrm{est})f_{\mathrm{start}})} \rfloor, \\ & s=0 \end{aligned} \end{equation} for $f_0>f_{\mathrm{start}}$, and \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & s= \lceil n - m/h_\mathrm{b}(q_\mathrm{est})f_{\mathrm{start}}\rceil, \\ & p=0 \end{aligned} \end{equation} for $f_0<f_{\mathrm{start}}$.
nodes.section: Appendix A: Workflow of the symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Compute numbers of punctured or shortened symbols reaching f_start.

nodes.name: Pick code maximizing raw bits
nodes.statement: The particular code among the set is then chosen in such a way that it has the maximal number of raw key bits in the extended key.
nodes.section: Appendix A: Workflow of the symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Pick the code with most raw key bits in the extended key.

nodes.name: Build extended keys
nodes.statement: Then the parties take blocks of their raw keys $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ of length $n-p-s$ and pad them with shortened and punctured symbols obtaining extended keys $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $\mathbf{y}_{\mathrm{ext}}$ of code block length $n$. In Fig.~\ref{fig:methods}(a) we denote this operation as $E(\cdot, S, P)$, where $S$ and $P$ are lists of positions for shortened and punctured symbols of length $s$ and $p$, respectively.
nodes.section: Appendix A: Workflow of the symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Pad raw-key blocks with shortened and punctured symbols to length n.

nodes.name: Choose positions S, P
nodes.statement: If it is possible, parties choose $P$ using position from special list, generated in advance with untainted puncturing technique~\cite{UntP}. Otherwise, the parties choose $P$ as well as $S$ with a synchronized PRNG.
nodes.section: Appendix A: Workflow of the symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Choose punctured positions from untainted list, else with synchronized PRNG.

nodes.name: Assign padded values
nodes.statement: All shortened symbols obtains zero values, while the values of the punctured bits come from the TRNG (independently on each side).
nodes.section: Appendix A: Workflow of the symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Shortened symbols are zero; punctured come from TRNG.

nodes.name: Store original positions
nodes.statement: The party that modifies its raw key (in our case it is Bob) also keeps original positions of shortened and punctured symbols as $S_0$ and $P_0$. These position are used in the final stage of the procedure.
nodes.section: Appendix A: Workflow of the symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Bob stores the original shortened/punctured positions.

nodes.name: Initialize error pattern and exchange syndromes
nodes.statement: The subsequent part of the procedure aims at reconstruction of a vector $\mathbf{e}_\mathrm{dec}$, which we call an error pattern, such that \begin{equation} \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbf{y}_{\mathrm{ext}}+\mathbf{e}_\mathrm{dec} ~ (\mathrm{mod}~2). \end{equation} In order to cope with this task, both Alice and Bob initialize the supposed error pattern $\mathbf{e}$ as the zero vector, calculate the syndromes $\mathbf{s_x}$ and $\mathbf{s_y}$ of their extended keys $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $\mathbf{y}_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and share the obtained syndromes with each other.
nodes.section: Appendix A: Workflow of the symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Set e=0, compute and exchange syndromes.

nodes.name: Decode relative syndrome
nodes.statement: Then each party performs belief-propagation decoding with the relative syndrome \begin{equation} \mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s_x}+\mathbf{s_y}~(\mathrm{mod}~2). \end{equation} We use an updated belief-propagation decoding algorithm (see below), which returns not only a resulting decoded vector $\mathbf{e}_\mathrm{dec}$ (that is ``none'' in the failure case), but also a set of bit positions $D$ of a fixed length $d$ which have the lowest LLR upon completion of the decoding. In other words, the updated decoding procedure returns $d$ positions of symbols with the most uncertainty in their values. Owing to the fact that both parties perform the same operation, they obtain the same output $\mathbf{e}_\mathrm{dec}$ and $D$.
nodes.section: Appendix A: Workflow of the symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Both run the updated BP decoder on the relative syndrome, getting e_dec and D.

nodes.name: Failure: disclose D
nodes.statement: In the case of a failure ($\mathbf{e}_\mathrm{dec}=\mathrm{none}$), the parties share the values of bits in the positions of $D$, update their supposed error pattern $\mathbf{e}$ in the positions from $D$ according to received values, \begin{equation} \mathbf{e}[D] = \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}}[D]+\mathbf{y}_{\mathrm{ext}}[D]~(\mathrm{mod}~2), \end{equation} and try to perform the decoding process again by marking positions in $D$ as shortened, which is crucial for the subsequent decoding procedure.
nodes.section: Appendix A: Workflow of the symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: On failure share bits at D, update e, mark D as shortened.

nodes.name: Repeat until convergence
nodes.statement: This sequence of operations is repeated until a convergence of belief-propagation decoding.
nodes.section: Appendix A: Workflow of the symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Repeat until BP decoding converges.

nodes.name: Bob corrects
nodes.statement: Then Bob applies error correction according to the obtained error pattern $\mathbf{e}_\mathrm{dec}$ by modulo 2 summation with his extended key $\mathbf{y}$.
nodes.section: Appendix A: Workflow of the symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Bob adds the error pattern to his extended key.

nodes.name: Strip and verify
nodes.statement: Finally, Bob excludes the symbols with initially shortened $S_0$ and punctured $P_0$ positions to obtain the corrected key $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{dec}}$ [we denote this operation $E^{-1}$ in Fig.~\ref{fig:methods}(a)], and parties move to the verification step with the original raw key $\mathbf{x}$ on Alice's side and its corrected version $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{dec}}$ on Bob's one.
nodes.section: Appendix A: Workflow of the symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Remove initial shortened/punctured symbols and pass to verification.

nodes.name: Initial LLRs
nodes.statement: We with a calculation of the initial LLRs for all symbol nodes. The corresponding vector is denoted as $\mathbf{r}^{(0)}$ and its elements are given by \begin{equation} \mathbf{r}^{(0)}[i] := \begin{cases} (-1)^{\mathbf{e}[i]} r_\mathrm{k}, &i\in K \\ (-1)^{\mathbf{e}[i]} r_\mathrm{s}, &i\in S \\ 0, &i\in P \end{cases}, \end{equation} where $K$ consists of raw key positions, such that \begin{equation} K\cup S\cup P=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}. \end{equation} Here, $r_\mathrm{k}$ is calculated using an estimated value of QBER, $\epsilon_\mathrm{est}$: \begin{equation} r_\mathrm{k} = \log\frac{1-q_\mathrm{est}}{q_\mathrm{est}}. \end{equation} The LLR value for shortened symbols $r_\mathrm{s}\gg 1$ and, in our implementation, we use $r_\mathrm{s}:=100$. The LLR for punctured symbols is zero, as there is no information about their values since they come from an independent true RNG
nodes.statement_short: Initialize LLRs for key, shortened and punctured positions.

nodes.name: Initial messages
nodes.statement: The initial messages from check nodes to symbol nodes are given by the initial values of corresponding LLRs as follows: \begin{equation} \mathbf{M}_{i\rightarrow j}^{(1)} := \mathbf{r}^{(0)}[i]. \end{equation} Here $i\in \mathcal{N}$ and $j\in A_i$, where $A_i$ is a set of symbol nodes connected to the $i$-th symbol node.
nodes.statement_short: Initial symbol-to-check messages equal initial LLRs.

nodes.name: Check-to-symbol messages
nodes.statement: Check nodes from messages back to the symbol node are realized in the following way: \begin{equation} \mathbf{M}_{i\leftarrow j}^{(k)} := 2\tanh^{-1}\left[\prod_{i'\in B_j/i}\frac{\mathbf{M}_{i'\rightarrow j}^{(k)}}{2}\right](-1)^{\mathbf{s}[j]}, \end{equation} where $j\in\mathcal{M}\equiv\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and $i\in B_j$, with $B_j$ being a set of symbol nodes connected to the $j$-th check node. We note that $\mathbf{M}_{i\leftarrow j}$ does not take into account $\mathbf{M}_{i\rightarrow j}$. Actually $\mathbf{M}_{i\leftarrow j}$ is the LLR of the $i$-th bit value based on satisfying the parity equation of the $j$-th row of the parity-check matrix $\mathbf{H}$, and the LLRs of all other symbol nodes taking part in this equation [see Fig.~\ref{fig:methods}(d)].
nodes.statement_short: Compute check-to-symbol messages via tanh rule with syndrome sign.

nodes.name: Update LLRs and hard decisions
nodes.statement: The symbol node updates its LLR using all of the messages coming from its check nodes: \begin{equation} \mathbf{r}^{(k)}[i] := \mathbf{r}^{(0)}[i]+\sum_{j\in A_i} \mathbf{M}_{i\leftarrow j}^{(k)} \end{equation} and it calculates current estimates for the bit values, \begin{equation} \mathbf{z}^{(k)}[i] := \begin{cases} 0, &\mathbf{r}^{(k)}[i]\geq0 \\ 1, &\mathbf{r}^{(k)}[i]<0 \end{cases}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Update symbol LLRs and take hard decisions.

nodes.name: Parity test
nodes.statement: If this estimate satisfies all parity equations, \begin{equation} \mathbf{H}\mathbf{z}^{(k)}=\mathbf{s}~(\mathrm{mod}~2), \end{equation} then the algorithm stops and returns the decoded vector $\mathbf{z}$
nodes.statement_short: Stop with z if all parity checks hold.

nodes.name: Averaged LLR magnitude
nodes.statement: As a stopping criterion, we consider behavior of averaged magnitude LLRs for symbols in nonshortened positions: \begin{equation} \hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(k)}:=\frac{1}{n-s}\sum_{i\in K\cup P}|\mathbf{r}^{(k)}[i]|. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Compute averaged |LLR| over nonshortened positions.

nodes.name: Stopping rule and D
nodes.statement: We stop the decoding and return ``none'' as the decoded vector if, for the current step $k$, the following inequality holds: \begin{equation} \hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(k)}\leq\frac{1}{\mathcal{N}}\sum_{j=k-\mathcal{N}}^{k-1}\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(j)}, \end{equation} where we use $\mathcal{N}:=5$. It can be interpreted as the end of a growth trend as far as our confidence in bit values. The algorithm also returns a $D$ that is a list of $d$ positions of symbols which has minimal values of LLR magnitude \begin{equation} D = \{i\;|\;|\mathbf{r}^{(k)}[i]|\leq |\mathbf{r}^{(k)}[j]| ~\forall j\notin D \}, \quad |D| = d. \end{equation} Otherwise, the algorithm goes to the next step.
nodes.statement_short: Return none and the d least reliable positions if averaged |LLR| stops growing.

nodes.name: Symbol-to-check messages
nodes.statement: According to the new LLRs, we update the messages from the symbol nodes to the check nodes: \begin{equation} \begin{split} \mathbf{M}_{i\rightarrow j}^{(k+1)} &:= \mathbf{r}^{(0)}[i]+\sum_{j'\in A_i/j} \mathbf{M}_{i\leftarrow j'}^{(k)} \\ &= \mathbf{r}^{(k)}[i]-\mathbf{M}_{i\leftarrow j}^{(k)} \end{split} \end{equation} where the counter of iterations is incremented, $k:=k+1$ [see Fig.~\ref{fig:methods}(e)], and the algorithm goes to the step with check nodes from messages back to symbol node [see Eq. (\ref{eq:step3})].
nodes.statement_short: Update symbol-to-check messages, increment k, loop.

nodes.name: Trivial bound L
nodes.statement: During the symmetric blind reconciliation Alice and Bob exchange \begin{equation} \mathcal{L} = 2(m+n_\mathrm{add}\;d) \end{equation} bits of information: each party transfers an $m$-bit syndrome and $n_\mathrm{add}\;d$ bits in additional communication rounds. Obviously, the information leakage could not be larger than $\mathcal{L}$.
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Total exchanged bits 2(m+n_add d) bound the leakage.

nodes.name: Two reasons
nodes.statement: Nevertheless, the actual leakage turns out to be lower (and given by Eq.\eqref{eq:leak}) for two reasons. First is that the $p_0$ punctured symbols due to their inherent uncertainty decrease the leakage from each of the syndromes from $m$ to $m-p_0$; and second is that the factor 2 in~\eqref{eq:len} could be omitted due to the fact that each pair of parity bits (one transferring from Alice to Bob, and the other -- in the opposite direction) can bring only one bit of valuable information to the eavesdropper. Next, we would like to focus on these two points.
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Outline: punctured symbols reduce syndrome leakage; factor 2 can be dropped.

nodes.name: Setup protocol
nodes.statement: Let us consider a symmetric blind reconciliation protocol for ${m}\times{n}$ parity-check matrix, $(n-s_0-p_0)$-bit sifted keys, $s_0$ shortened, and $p_0$ punctured bits. Recall that the punctured symbols are the bits with values coming from independent TRNGs on both sides. The consideration of the puncturing technique is greatly simplified in untainted puncturing ~\cite{UntP}, which is employed in our scheme.
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Fix the protocol parameters with untainted puncturing.

nodes.name: Split syndrome positions
nodes.statement: In the untainted puncturing, each of the check nodes of the Tanner graph (corresponding the employed parity-check matrix) is connected with, at most, one punctured symbol. This implies that it is possible to split al ofl the syndrome bits' positions $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ into the subsets $F$ and $\overline{F}$ where $F$ contains $p_0$ check nodes indices of those which are connected with the punctured bits, and the subset $\overline{F}\equiv \{1,2,\ldots,m\}/F$ contains all of the remaining syndrome-bit positions.
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Split syndrome positions into F (connected to punctured bits) and its complement.

nodes.name: Punctured syndrome bits leak nothing
nodes.statement: Since each of the syndrome-bit values $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{x}}[F]$ and $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{y}}[F]$ is obtained as the result of a modulo-2 summation of nonpunctured symbols and a single punctured bit (which is completely random at each side), the disclosure of $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{x}}[F]$ and $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{y}}[F]$ in the public channel does not bring any valuable information to the eavesdropper. One can imagine that bits of $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{x}}[F]$ and $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{y}}[F]$ are transferred separately from all other public communications that is considered further. Thus, the information leakage does not exceed $2(m-p_0+n_\mathrm{add}\;d)$ bits.
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Syndrome bits on F are uniformly random, so leakage is at most 2(m-p0+n_add d).

nodes.name: Random puncturing remark
nodes.statement: We wish to remark that the case of random puncturing, where the \emph{positions} for punctured symbols are chosen with synchronised PRNGs, could be treated in a similar way, but in this case an additional information about the Tanner graph construction method has to be taken into account. One has to show that it is always possible to choose $p_0$ syndrome bits whose values are statistically independent from the $n-p_0$ values of symbols that are not punctured.
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Random puncturing would need an extra independence argument.

nodes.name: Recall Lo's framework
nodes.statement: The second statement about the factor 2 in Eq.~\eqref{eq:len} is closely related to a similar question regarding to the one of the first information reconciliation protocols -- Cascade~\cite{Cascade1_orig}, where Alice and Bob also exchange with parity bits of some blocks of their keys in a symmetrical way. A rigorous examination of this question related to the BB84 protocol is considered by H.-K. Lo in Ref.~\cite{LO_decoupling}. In his work Lo considers the \emph{adaptive symmetric method for error correction} (which we will refer to simply as \emph{adaptive symmetric error correction}) --- the generalized information reconciliation protocol which includes Cascade and the symmetric blind reconciliation. Next, we provide its definition.
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Relate the factor-2 question to Lo's adaptive symmetric error correction.

nodes.name: Quoted definition
nodes.statement: \emph{Definition}~(adapted from Ref.~\cite{LO_decoupling}). Adaptive symmetric error correction is an iterative procedure applied to Alice's $n$-bit string $\mathbf{x}$ and Bob's $n$-bit string $\mathbf{y}$ (which is a corrupted version of $\mathbf{x}$). where the rounds of operations given below are performed. \begin{itemize} \item Round 1. Alice picks an $n$-bit string ${\bf a}_1$, and broadcasts ${\bf a}_1$ and the parity $p_{\mathbf{x},1} = {\bf a}_1 \cdot \mathbf{x}~({\rm mod}~2)$. Bob broadcasts the parity $p_{\mathbf{y},1} = {\bf a}_1 \cdot \mathbf{y}~({\rm mod}~2)$. Alice and Bob compute the relative parity $r_1=p_{\mathbf{y},1}-p_{\mathbf{x},1}~({\rm mod}~2)$. \item Round $i$ ($i>1$). Alice picks an $i$-bit string ${\bf a}_i$, where the choice of ${\bf a}_i$ may depend on the strings $\{{\bf a}_j|j<i\}$ and the relative parities $\{r_j|j<i\}$ (but not on the individual parities, $\{p_{\mathbf{x},j}|j<i\}$ and $\{p_{\mathbf{y},j}|j<i\}$). Then Alice broadcasts ${\bf a}_i$ and the parity $p_{\mathbf{x},i} = {\bf a}_i \cdot \mathbf{x}~({\rm mod}~2)$. Bob broadcasts the parity $p_{y,i} = {\bf a}_i \cdot \mathbf{y}~({\rm mod}~2)$. Alice and Bob compute the relative parity $r_i=p_{\mathbf{y},1}-p_{\mathbf{x},1}~({\rm mod}~2)$. \end{itemize} After some number $N$ of necessary rounds, Bob corrects the errors in his string $\mathbf{y}$ by applying a recovery operator \begin{equation} \mathbf{z}:=\mathrm{Recover}(\mathbf{y}, \{r_i\}_{i=1}^N). \end{equation} Ideally, $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{x}$ and Alice and Bob will now share the same string $\mathbf{x}$.
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Recall the definition of adaptive symmetric error correction.

nodes.name: 2N bits exchanged
nodes.statement: One can see that, in the described protocol, Alice and Bob exchange with $2N$ bits of information: $N$ bits goes from Alice to Bob, and $N$ bits -- in the opposite direction.
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: The protocol exchanges 2N bits.

nodes.name: Leakage equals N
nodes.statement: From an overall key generation balance point of view, this scenario is equivalent to the situation, where the information leakage in the adaptive symmetric error correction is equal to $N$.
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Lo's result means effective leakage is N.

nodes.name: Return to protocol
nodes.statement: Now we return to the symmetric blind reconciliation. As it was shown, the communication of $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{x}}[F]$ and $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{y}}[F]$ can be considered separately since none of these bits bring any valuable information to the eavesdropper.
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Discard the F syndrome bits as leak-free.

nodes.name: Syndromes as rounds
nodes.statement: The exchange of the remaining syndrome bits $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{x}}[\overline{F}]$ and $\mathbf{s}_{\mathbf{y}}[\overline{F}]$, can be regarded as the first $m-p_0$ rounds of the adaptive symmetric error correction: for each syndrome bit, the string ${\bf a}_i$ from the definition is the corresponding row of the employed parity-check matrix.
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Remaining syndrome bits are the first m-p0 rounds.

nodes.name: D depends only on relative parities
nodes.statement: The syndrome decoding algorithm~\eqref{eq:synddec} either converges and allows Bob to perform a recovery of $\mathbf{x}$ or returns a set of positions $D$ for the new communication round. Note that the set $D$ is obtained as a result of the syndrome decoding executed for the relative syndrome $\mathbf{s}$. By its definition [see Eq.~\eqref{eq:relsyndr}], the relative syndrome consists of relative parities; therefore the choice of positions for the set $D$ is in agreement with the definition of adaptive symmetric error correction.
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: D comes from the relative syndrome, consistent with the definition.

nodes.name: Extra rounds as d rounds
nodes.statement: Each of the additional communication rounds of the symmetric blind reconciliation with respect to the set $D$, can be regarded as $|D|=d$ of communication rounds in the definition of the adaptive symmetric error correction. Namely, the string ${\bf a}_i$ has all zeros except for a single one at the position $D_j$ (here, $i$ is the number of the round in the general sequence, and $j$ is the index of the element inside the set $D$ of length $d$).
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: Each extra round is d unit-vector rounds.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus, the completion of the symmetric blind reconciliation with $n_{\rm add}$ additional rounds corresponds to the adaptive symmetric error correction with $N=m-p_0+n_{\rm add}d$ rounds, and the information leakage given by expression~\eqref{eq:leak}.
nodes.section: Appendix C: Security of symmetric blind reconciliation
nodes.statement_short: So N=m-p0+n_add d and the leakage formula holds.
